en: *Treatise on the Northern School of the Mahāyāna*, Scroll One:
The Mahāyāna Mind. The Mahāyāna mind:
I do not even give rise to the thought of giving; how much less so the thoughts of stinginess and greed?
I do not even give rise to the thought of maintaining precepts, let alone the thought of transgressing them;
I do not even give rise to the thought of patience, let alone the thought of killing;
I do not even give rise to the thought of diligence, let alone the thought of indolence.
I do not even give rise to a mind of meditative concentration, much less a distracted mind;
I do not even give rise to a mind of wisdom, much less a deluded mind;
I do not even give rise to a mind of heaven, much less a mind of hell.
I do not yet give rise to a heart of compassion, much less a heart of malice;
I do not yet give rise to a pure heart, much less a defiled heart;
I do not yet give rise to a joyful heart, much less a heart of anger and resentment.
I do not even give rise to a mind of benefit, much less a mind of plunder;
I do not even give rise to a vast mind, much less a narrow-minded one;
I do not even give rise to a mind of emptiness, much less a mind of dogmatic attachment to views.
I do not yet give rise to an upright mind, let alone a crooked one;
I do not yet give rise to a true mind, let alone an inverted one;
I do not yet give rise to the Mahāyāna mind, let alone the Śrāvaka mind.
I do not even give rise to the mind of a bodhisattva, let alone the mind of an ordinary person;
I do not even give rise to the mind of enlightenment, let alone the mind of affliction;
I do not even give rise to the mind of liberation, let alone the mind of bondage.
I do not yet give rise to the thought of nirvana, much less the thought of birth and death;
thus he spoke these verses again:
"Sorrow arises from the mind, joy arises from the mind; if one is deluded regarding the mind..."
That which has patterns and characters is called birth-and-death; that which has no patterns and no characters is called nirvāṇa.
That which has speech and explanation is called birth-and-death; that which has no speech and no explanation is called nirvāṇa.
That which involves cultivation and study is called birth-and-death; that which involves neither cultivation nor study is called nirvāṇa.
To have wisdom and insight is called birth-and-death; to lack wisdom and insight is called nirvāṇa.
To have aversion and dharmas is called birth-and-death; to lack aversion and dharmas is called nirvāṇa.
To have precepts and discipline is called birth-and-death; to lack precepts and discipline is called nirvāṇa.
That which is conditioned and active is called birth-and-death; that which is unconditioned and inactive is called nirvāṇa.
To sever the afflictions is called birth-and-death; not severing the afflictions is called nirvāṇa.
To perceive liberation is called birth-and-death; not perceiving liberation is called nirvāṇa.
To perceive nirvāṇa is called saṃsāra; not perceiving nirvāṇa is called nirvāṇa.
To feel aversion toward the world is called saṃsāra; not feeling aversion toward the world is called nirvāṇa.
To delight in the Mahāyāna is called saṃsāra; not delighting in the Mahāyāna is called nirvāṇa.
To perceive the pāramitās is called saṃsāra; not perceiving the pāramitās is called nirvāṇa.
Thus, there are ten [aspects] of the Mahāyāna.
